claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in structural materials for fusion plasma-facing components are governed by dislocation stability and mobility.
Grain-boundary structure and composition influence dislocation stability and mobility.
The initial material is a polycrystalline tungsten alloy with grain size and composition typical of plasma-facing components.
Doping with selected elements can introduce controlled variations in grain-boundary structure and composition.
The selected doping elements are known to alter grain-boundary cohesion.
The selected doping elements are known to alter dislocation mobility.
A temperature range of 1000–1500°C is representative of fusion-reactor conditions relevant to this comparison.
Doping elements segregate to tungsten grain boundaries.
Segregated dopants alter the ease with which dislocations move across or interact with grain boundaries.
Changes in grain-boundary cohesion and dislocation mobility affect the ability of tungsten alloys to accommodate plastic strain and resist fracture at high temperature.
Doped tungsten alloys will exhibit greater plastic strain than undoped tungsten alloys under otherwise identical high-temperature loading.
Doped tungsten alloys will exhibit greater toughness than undoped tungsten alloys under otherwise identical high-temperature loading.
The hypothesized relationship applies to tungsten alloys having grain sizes and compositions typical of plasma-facing components.
The hypothesized relationship applies at temperatures up to 1500°C.
The specific dopant elements and concentrations needed to produce the predicted improvement are not established.
The hypothesis does not account for interactions between dopants and plasma exposure.
